t: A risk has a 1% chance of a ₹20 lakh loss and, independently, a 5% chance of a ₹2 lakh loss in a year. The expected annual loss is:
10,000 independent policies each have a 1% chance of a total loss of ₹1 lakh. The expected aggregate loss and its approximate standard deviation are:
Claims on a policy are Poisson with mean 1 per year. The probability of exactly two claims in a year is approximately (e⁻¹ ≈ 0.368):
Claim counts follow a negative binomial distribution with mean 0.20 and parameter β = 0.10, for which variance = mean × (1 + β). The variance is:
e: Variance = 0.20 × 1.10 = 0.22, exceeding the mean — the over-dispersion that distinguishes negative binomial from Poisson.

t: Each of 4,000 policies has claim frequency 0.05 and expected severity ₹60,000. The expected aggregate loss for the portfolio is:
Aggregate losses S (₹ lakh) take the values 0, 100 and 300 with probabilities 0.6, 0.3 and 0.1. The pure premium for a stop-loss cover paying the excess of S over ₹100 lakh is:
e: E[(S − 100)⁺] = 0.1 × (300 − 100) = ₹20 lakh; only the ₹300 lakh outcome exceeds the attachment.

t: Annual severity trend is 6% and the trend period is 2.5 years. The severity trend factor to apply is approximately:
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). Trend factor = 1.06^2.5 = 1.06² × 1.06^0.5 ≈ 1.1236 × 1.0296 ≈ 1.157.

t: For the same distribution (0, 100, 300 ₹ lakh with probabilities 0.6, 0.3, 0.1), the expected aggregate loss E[S] is:
Which of the following statements about a lognormal severity distribution is correct?
o: Its mean is less than its median
Its mean exceeds its median because of positive skewness
It is symmetric about the mean
e: If ln X is normal with parameters μ and σ², the median is e^μ while the mean is e^(μ + σ²/2), which is larger; the distribution is right-skewed and positive.

t: For any mixed Poisson claim-count distribution (Poisson rate varying across risks), the variance of the number of claims is:
o: Always greater than or equal to the mean
e: Var[N] = E[Λ] + Var[Λ] ≥ E[N]; equality holds only when all risks share the same rate (pure Poisson).

t: Aggregate losses are approximately normal with mean ₹200 lakh and standard deviation ₹25 lakh. The probability that losses exceed ₹250 lakh is approximately (Φ(2) ≈ 0.977):
Diversification across a large number of risks reduces relative variability only if the risks are:
o: All located in the same region
All of the same sum insured
e: The variance of the average falls as 1/n only for independent risks; correlated exposures (e.g. one earthquake zone) do not diversify and need reinsurance or accumulation limits.

t: The insurer's own experience indicates a +9% rate change and is assigned credibility 0.50. The complement (trended present rates) indicates +2%. The credibility-weighted rate change is:
Projected frequency is 0.06 and projected severity ₹25,000; LAE is 10% of losses; fixed expense ₹150 per exposure; variable expense 22% and profit 3% of premium. The indicated rate per exposure is:
Applying both a loss development factor and a trend factor to accident-year losses does NOT double count because:
o: Development is applied only to paid losses and trend only to incurred
Development projects the emergence of losses already occurred to their ultimate value, whereas trend moves the cost level of those losses to the future rating period
Regulators allow only one of the two
Trend is applied before development, cancelling the overlap
e: The 'overlap fallacy' argument fails: development measures reporting/settlement completeness, trend measures change in cost level; both are needed for a full projection.

t: Under the standard deviation premium principle P = E[S] + α·SD[S] with α = 0.5, a risk with E[S] = ₹8 lakh and SD[S] = ₹2 lakh has premium:
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). P = 8 + 0.5 × 2 = ₹9.0 lakh; unlike the expected value principle this loading reflects the risk's variability.

t: An exponential regression of ln(average severity) on time gives a slope of 0.05 per year. The implied annual severity trend is approximately:
e: Annual trend = e^0.05 − 1 ≈ 1.0513 − 1 ≈ 5.1%; the slope of a log-linear fit is a continuously compounded rate.

t: All experience-period premium was written at a single rate level. Since then, rate changes of +4%, −2% and +6% have been implemented in succession. The on-level factor to bring the experience-period premium to the current rate level is approximately:
e: Cumulative factor = 1.04 × 0.98 × 1.06 ≈ 1.0804; rate changes compound multiplicatively, not additively (which would give 1.08).

t: An annual motor policy from 1 April 2025 covers two cars, and a separate six-month policy from 1 April 2025 covers one car. The total earned exposure (car-years) for calendar year 2025 from these policies is:
e: Two cars × 9/12 year = 1.5 car-years, plus one car × 6/12 = 0.5 car-year; total = 2.0 car-years earned in 2025.

t: Which of the following is NOT typically a driver of claim frequency trend in motor insurance?
o: Changes in traffic density and road conditions
e: Repair cost inflation affects severity, not the number of claims; the other factors influence how many claims arise or are reported.

t: Under the 1/24th method, annual policies written during March are assumed to incept on 15 March. The fraction of their premium that is unearned at 31 December of the same year is:
e: From 15 March to 31 December is 9.5 months = 19/24 earned, so 5/24 is unearned; the method approximates uniform writing within each month.

t: An insurer's target return on surplus is 15%, its premium-to-surplus ratio is 2:1, and investment income is estimated at 5% of premium. The underwriting profit provision needed in the rate (as % of premium) is:
e: Required total return = 15% of surplus = 7.5% of premium (surplus is half of premium); less 5% investment income leaves 2.5% underwriting profit.

t: Basic-limit losses in the experience period are ₹80 lakh and the selected excess loss factor (to restore losses above the basic limit on a long-term expected basis) is 1.15. The total losses used in the indication are:
e: 80 × 1.15 = ₹92 lakh; the excess factor replaces actual volatile large losses with a stable expected provision.

t: The basic limit for a liability line is ₹5 lakh. A single claim of ₹8 lakh is recorded. In an increased-limits analysis this claim contributes:
o: ₹5 lakh to basic-limit losses and ₹3 lakh to the excess layer above ₹5 lakh
e: Losses are capped at the basic limit for basic-limit experience; the portion above the limit belongs to the excess layer used to derive increased limits factors.

t: Claim frequency per exposure rose from 0.0500 to 0.0551 over exactly two years. The implied annual frequency trend is approximately:
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). Two-year factor = 0.0551/0.0500 = 1.102; annual trend = √1.102 − 1 ≈ 1.05 − 1 = 5%.

t: A premium discount (expense gradation) is offered to large commercial risks because:
o: It is required by the Insurance Act 1938
Fixed expenses form a smaller percentage of a large premium, so a flat percentage expense loading would overcharge them
e: Policy issuance and servicing costs do not rise in proportion to premium; the discount reduces the expense loading percentage for successive layers of premium.

t: A risk is assigned credibility 0.35 and its actual-to-expected loss ratio is 0.60. The experience modification factor is:
In a retrospective rating plan the basic premium is expressed as a factor of standard premium. With standard premium ₹50 lakh and a basic premium factor of 0.20, the basic premium is:
e: Basic premium = 50 × 0.20 = ₹10 lakh; it covers expenses (other than LAE and taxes) plus the net insurance charge.

t: Retro formula R = (10 + 1.10 L) × 1.03 (₹ lakh) with a maximum premium of ₹55 lakh. The level of incurred losses L at which the maximum premium is first reached is approximately:
e: Set (10 + 1.1L) × 1.03 = 55 → 10 + 1.1L = 53.40 → L = 43.40/1.1 ≈ ₹39.5 lakh; losses beyond this do not raise the premium.

t: In split-plan experience rating, the 'D-ratio' is:
o: The ratio of expected primary losses to expected total losses
The ratio of actual to expected losses
The ratio of paid to incurred losses
e: The D-ratio converts expected total losses into the expected primary portion so that actual primary losses can be compared with their expectation.

t: Which statement about Bühlmann credibility Z = n/(n + K) is INCORRECT?
o: Z increases toward 1 as the number of observations n grows
K equals the expected process variance divided by the variance of hypothetical means
K changes with the number of years of data observed
A larger variance between risks (VHM) lowers K and raises Z
e: K is a property of the population (EPV/VHM) and does not depend on n; only Z changes as more data accumulate.

t: The expected process variance for a risk is 900 and the variance of hypothetical means across risks is 300. For a risk with 9 years of observations, the Bühlmann credibility is:
Which individual risk rating technique relies on the underwriter's judgement of risk characteristics rather than on the insured's statistical loss record?
e: Schedule rating applies judgemental credits and debits for features such as fire protection or safety management; the other methods use the insured's actual losses.

t: For a reported claim, the case-incurred amount is ₹12 lakh and payments to date total ₹7 lakh. The outstanding case reserve is:
e: Case incurred = paid + case reserve, so the reserve = 12 − 7 = ₹5 lakh.

t: Cumulative incurred (₹ lakh): AY1: 200 (12m), 260 (24m), 273 (36m); AY2: 220 (12m), 275 (24m); AY3: 250 (12m). With volume-weighted factors and no development beyond 36 months, the AY3 ultimate is approximately:
In the same triangle, the chain-ladder IBNR for AY2 is approximately:
The principle that allows an insurer who has paid a claim to step into the insured's shoes and recover from a liable third party is:
e: ★ Core fact (asked across III papers). Subrogation is a corollary of indemnity; it does not apply to life or personal accident (benefit) policies.

t: Combining the previous two questions, the total chain-ladder IBNR for AY2 and AY3 together is approximately:
e: AY3 IBNR ≈ 334 − 250 = 84; AY2 IBNR ≈ 13.75; total ≈ ₹98 lakh.

t: Under the Bornhuetter-Ferguson method an accident year at 12 months has a reported-to-ultimate factor of 3.0 and an a priori expected ultimate of ₹90 lakh. The BF IBNR is:
e: Unreported proportion = 1 − 1/3 = 2/3; IBNR = 90 × 2/3 = ₹60 lakh, regardless of what has actually been reported so far.

t: An actual-versus-expected test: reported losses for an accident year were ₹100 lakh a year ago and the selected age-to-age factor for that interval is 1.50. Actual reported losses now are ₹165 lakh. The result is:
o: Adverse emergence of ₹15 lakh relative to expectation
e: Expected reported = 100 × 1.5 = 150; actual 165 exceeds this by ₹15 lakh, suggesting the factor or ultimate may need to be revisited.

t: Incremental paid losses for an accident year are ₹100 lakh (12m), ₹50 lakh (24m) and ₹20 lakh (36m). The cumulative paid losses at 36 months are:
e: Cumulative = 100 + 50 + 20 = ₹170 lakh; development factors are computed on cumulative, not incremental, amounts.

t: All accident years in a triangle have reached at least 36 months and their cumulative reported losses total ₹500 crore. If the actuary raises the tail factor from 1.02 to 1.05, the total reserve increases by approximately:
e: Increase = 500 × (1.05 − 1.02) = ₹15 crore, showing how sensitive long-tail reserves are to the tail assumption.

t: Compared with a claims-made policy, an occurrence-basis liability policy generally requires:
o: IBNR only for the first year
A larger IBNR provision, because claims may be reported many years after the policy period
e: Occurrence cover responds to events in the policy period whenever reported, so unreported claims can emerge for years; claims-made cover limits this exposure.

t: Which of the following is generally a sign that an insurer's carried reserves have been deficient?
o: Consistent favourable runoff in successive years
Repeated adverse development, where re-estimated ultimates for old years keep rising
e: If ultimates for prior accident years must be increased year after year, earlier reserves were too low; favourable runoff would indicate redundancy.

t: Class A is rated ₹2,000 and class B ₹4,000. The book moves from a 50/50 mix to 30% class A and 70% class B with no rate change. The average premium per exposure changes by approximately:
e: Old average = 3,000; new = 0.3 × 2,000 + 0.7 × 4,000 = 3,400; change = +13.3% purely from the mix shift, which is why premium trend is monitored.

t: In a life insurance contract, insurable interest must exist:
o: At the time of the claim only
Both at inception and at claim
e: ★ Core fact (asked across III papers). Life: at inception only. Marine: at the time of loss. Fire and motor: at both inception and loss.

t: The 'causality' (or intuitive relationship) criterion for a rating variable requires that:
o: The variable must be the direct physical cause of every loss
The variable has at least 1,082 claims
The variable is chosen by regulators
There is a plausible, explainable connection between the variable and expected losses, even if not strictly causal
e: Public and regulatory acceptance is easier when the variable (e.g. engine capacity, construction type) has an intuitive link to loss propensity, not merely a statistical correlation.

t: Which of the following would most clearly fail the 'social acceptability' criterion for a rating variable in India?
o: Religion or caste of the proposer
e: Variables such as religion or caste are socially and legally unacceptable for rating irrespective of any statistical association; vehicle and location characteristics are standard.

t: Using the loss ratio relativity method: a class has a loss ratio of 80% against an overall loss ratio of 64%, and its current relativity is 1.20. The indicated relativity is:
e: Indicated change to the relativity = 0.80/0.64 = 1.25; new relativity = 1.20 × 1.25 = 1.50.

t: Under the Indian motor own-damage no-claim bonus (NCB) scale, a policyholder with two consecutive claim-free years whose base OD premium is ₹10,000 pays an OD premium of:
e: The NCB scale is 20%, 25%, 35%, 45% and 50% for one to five claim-free years; two years earns 25%, so premium = 10,000 × 0.75 = ₹7,500. NCB applies only to the OD component.
